lead: A cell stores chemical energy and gives it back as electricity. The lead-acid cell does this with two lead-based plates dipped in dilute sulfuric acid. It is cheap, it can push out a huge burst of current for cranking, and it survives hundreds of charge and discharge cycles. Six such cells in one plastic box make the 12 V battery that every petrol and diesel car carries. This chapter opens the box: the plates, the separator, the acid, and the two reactions — one going out on discharge, the reverse going in on charge.
prereq: You need: the battery's place among vehicle loads from Chapter 1.1, and basic oxidation and reduction from school chemistry.

sections.h3: One cell, then a battery of six

blocks.text: A cell is one complete chemical unit: two plates with the electrolyte between them. A battery is one or more cells joined and sold as one package. A car battery holds six cells inside a single case.

In series means the same current flows through every cell, and the cell voltages add. A fully charged lead-acid cell rests at about 2.1 V on open circuit. Six cells give 6 × 2.1 V = 12.6 V. The "12 V" on the label is nominal: a healthy battery at rest reads close to 12.6 V and slides towards 12.0 V as charge is used.

blocks.where: n is the number of cells in series (6 in an automotive battery); V_cell is the open-circuit voltage of one fully charged cell, about 2.1 V; V_battery is the battery terminal voltage at rest, in volts.

blocks.text: The series connection gives the 12.6 V the starter needs (see Chapter 1.7); the large plate area and the few milliohms of internal resistance let the pack push out hundreds of amperes, with the terminal voltage sagging by a volt or two.

sections.h3: Inside a cell: plates, separator, acid and case

blocks.text: A cell is a stack of alternating plates. The negative plate is a lead grid filled with spongy lead (Pb): grey, soft and very porous, so the acid touches a huge surface area. The positive plate is a similar grid whose active material is lead dioxide (PbO<sub>2</sub>), a dark brown powder. The grid itself is only the conductor; it carries current to the plate lug.

Two plate families exist. Plante plates are formed by converting the lead plate itself into active material through repeated cycling. They are thick and hold less energy per kilogram, but they last long, so they suit standby work. Pasted plates are made by spreading a paste of lead oxides onto a cast lead-alloy grid and then forming it by charging. They store more energy per kilogram and are what nearly every vehicle battery uses.

A porous separator lies between each pair of opposite plates. It lets ions pass but stops the plates touching, which would short the cell. Wood, rubber, glass fibre and plastics such as polyethylene have all been used.

The electrolyte is dilute sulfuric acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in water). When fully charged its specific gravity is about 1.26 to 1.28. Specific gravity is the density of the liquid divided by the density of water, so 1.28 means the acid is 1.28 times as dense as water.

Everything sits in one compartment of a hard rubber or polypropylene case. Partitions divide the case into six cells. The cover carries the terminals — the positive post is deliberately made larger than the negative — and vented caps that let gas escape and water be added.

sections.h3: Discharge and charge: one reaction, run both ways

blocks.text: Discharge turns chemical energy into electrical energy. At the negative plate, lead gives up electrons and becomes lead sulfate. At the positive plate, lead dioxide takes electrons and also becomes lead sulfate.
Pb + HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> → PbSO<sub>4</sub> + H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>   (negative plate, discharge)
blocks.where: Pb is spongy lead; HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is the bisulfate ion from the acid; PbSO<sub>4</sub> is lead sulfate; e<sup>−</sup> is an electron released to the external circuit. This is oxidation.
PbO<sub>2</sub> is lead dioxide; H<sup>+</sup> is the hydrogen ion; H<sub>2</sub>O is water. This is reduction, taking the two electrons the negative plate released.
the left side is the charged state (lead, lead dioxide, sulfuric acid); the right side is the discharged state (lead sulfate on both plates plus water).

blocks.text: Both plates end up coated with lead sulfate. The acid is a reactant, not just a conducting liquid: it is consumed while water is produced, so the electrolyte weakens and its specific gravity falls. That fall is what a hydrometer reads (see Chapter 1.3), and what battery sensing in Unit 3 uses to estimate state of charge.

Charging reverses every term: 2PbSO4 + 2H2O → Pb + PbO2 + 2H2SO4. The positive plate stays positive; the charger simply pushes current the other way through the cell, so the reactions run backwards and the acid is restored. The charger must apply more than 12.6 V to drive current in — the regulation side of this is in Chapter 1.4.

sections.h3: Voltage, gassing and the faults that age a battery

blocks.text: Open-circuit cell voltage stays near 2.1 V for most of the discharge and then falls steeply at the end. Under load the terminal voltage is lower by I × R<sub>internal</sub>, where I is the current drawn in amperes and R<sub>internal</sub> is the internal resistance in ohms.

Above about 2.3 to 2.4 V per cell (roughly 13.8 to 14.4 V for the whole battery) the charging current starts splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen. This is gassing, not boiling. Water is lost, the level drops, and the gas mixture is explosive, so vents stay clear and sparks stay away.

items: Sulfation: lead sulfate left standing crystallises. Hard crystals do not convert back on charge, so capacity is lost permanently. Storing a battery discharged is the usual cause.
Stratification: acid is denser than water and sinks, so the bottom of the cell is stronger than the top and the plates work unevenly. Driving, and charging, stirs the liquid.
Self-discharge: a battery standing idle loses charge by internal leakage, a few percent a month, faster when warm.

figure.caption: One cell is a negative plate, a separator, a positive plate and dilute sulfuric acid in a case; six cells in series give about 12.6 V. Notice that the two plate types alternate and the acid touches both.

spec.aria: A cell stack shows a negative lead plate, a separator, a positive lead dioxide plate and dilute sulfuric acid electrolyte, with six such cells giving about 12.6 V.

examples.question: A fully charged lead-acid cell rests at 2.1 V on open circuit. (a) Find the open-circuit voltage of an automotive battery that contains six such cells in series. (b) Later, one cell develops an internal short circuit and behaves as a plain conductor. Find the new battery voltage.
steps: The six cells are in series, so the voltages add: V_battery = n × V_cell.
Healthy case: n = 6 and V_cell = 2.1 V, so V_battery = 6 × 2.1 V = 12.6 V.
A shorted cell contributes 0 V and no longer reacts, so only 5 cells are active: n = 5.
Check the direction: fewer active cells means a lower voltage, and 10.5 V is lower than 12.6 V, as expected.
examples.answer: The battery reads 12.6 V when healthy and 10.5 V with one cell shorted.
examples.check:
cells = 6
v_cell = 2.1
healthy = cells * v_cell
faulty = (cells - 1) * v_cell
print(round(healthy, 2))
print(round(faulty, 2))

traps: The positive plate of a charged cell is lead dioxide, PbO₂; the negative plate is spongy lead, Pb. Swapping them is the commonest error in this chapter.
A cell is about 2.1 V, not 2.0 V, and a 12 V battery has six cells. Six times 2.1 V is 12.6 V at rest; 12 V is only the nominal label.
The acid is a reactant, not just a conductor. It is consumed on discharge, which is why specific gravity falls and can be used to read state of charge.
The plate that is positive on discharge stays positive on charge. Charging reverses the reaction direction, not the plate polarity.
Gassing is not boiling. It is the electrolysis of water and it starts above about 2.3 to 2.4 V per cell (roughly 13.8 to 14.4 V for the whole battery).

quiz.q: Name the active material of the positive and of the negative plate in a charged lead-acid cell.
quiz.a: Positive plate: lead dioxide, PbO₂, dark brown. Negative plate: spongy lead, Pb, grey and porous.

quiz.q: How many cells are in a 12 V automotive battery, and what is the open-circuit voltage of one cell?
quiz.a: Six cells in series. Each rests at about 2.1 V, so the battery reads about 12.6 V.

quiz.q: Why does the specific gravity of the electrolyte fall during discharge?
quiz.a: The discharge reaction consumes sulfuric acid and produces water, so the liquid becomes less dense. Specific gravity drops from about 1.26–1.28 towards about 1.12.

quiz.q: State the difference between Plante and pasted plates.
quiz.a: Plante plates have their active material formed from the lead plate itself, giving a thick, durable plate of lower capacity per kilogram. Pasted plates carry a paste of lead oxides on a cast grid, give higher capacity, and are used in vehicles.

quiz.q: A 12 V battery has two cells with internal short circuits. Each healthy cell gives 2.1 V on open circuit. Find the terminal voltage.
quiz.a: Four healthy cells remain: n = 4, V = 4 × 2.1 V = 8.4 V.

quiz.q: A battery is left flat for six months and then charged for a full day. It still cannot crank the engine. Explain using the cell reactions and name the fault.
quiz.a: The lead sulfate on both plates crystallised into a hard form that does not convert back to Pb and PbO₂ during charging. The fault is sulfation: active material and acid are permanently lost, so capacity is gone even though the charger and the wiring are fine.

beyond: Not for the exam. Batteries have moved past the flooded cell: absorbed glass mat (AGM) and gel types hold the acid so it cannot stratify or spill, and lead-carbon designs add carbon to the negative plate to survive the repeated partial charging of start-stop traffic. Research follows grid alloys, with calcium replacing antimony to cut self-discharge, and estimating state of charge from impedance, which is where Unit 3 sensing ends up. Search for "AGM separator", "lead-carbon negative plate" and "electrochemical impedance spectroscopy battery".
